title: Living ashtpadi 17
hookLine: truth in Sukhmani is lived, not argued

cards: Somewhere online, right now, two people are arguing about what's true. They've been at it for forty replies. Each has links, each has receipts, neither has moved an inch.
Meanwhile, somewhere else, a woman is quietly returning a wallet she found, with every bill still inside, and nobody will ever post about it. Which of those two scenes has more truth in it?
Guru Nanak put the answer into a single line, and it's the key to the seventeenth ashtpadi.

teach.b: This week the seventeenth ashtpadi gave us three pictures. Truth runs through all time: aad sach. Truth runs through everything: true His feet, true who touches them, the true court.
And truth spreads to people: the devotee becomes true by contact.
Notice what's missing: no argument, no proof. Sukhmani doesn't try to convince anyone that truth exists. It assumes truth, and asks what happens to a life that touches it.
Guru Nanak said it outright in Sri Raag, in a line many Sikhs know: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Sach aachaar. Aachaar means conduct, how you actually live.
So above truth as an idea sits truth as a habit. That's an unusual ranking. Many people think of truth mainly as something to know or defend; Gurbani puts the weight on something to do.
It goes back to the beginning of Japji, which you heard at the start of this path.
Guru Nanak's very first question there is: kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai? How does one become sachiaar, a truthful one? Not how do we prove what's true, but how do we become it.
And Japji's answer isn't a debate. It's a way of walking: in the order of the One's will.
So living ashtpadi 17 isn't about winning arguments for truth, even good ones. It's about the wallet. The honest timesheet.
The apology without excuses. The plain answer when a dodge would be easier. Truth, in Sukhmani, is a thing you do with your hands.

how: Sikhs often cite Guru Nanak's teaching that truthful living stands above truth itself, and Japji Sahib, recited each morning, opens its first stanza with the question of how to become sachiaar, truthful.

o: a scholar who argues for the truth
a truthful one, who lives the truth
a judge who decides what is true

s: Sukhmani's seventeenth ashtpadi sets out arguments proving truth exists
it assumes truth and asks what happens to a life that touches it.
Guru Nanak placed truthful living above truth as an idea
truth is higher than all, and higher still is sach aachaar.
Japji's first question is how to prove what's true
it asks kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai: how does one become truthful?

games.q: you're forty replies into an online argument about what's true. what would living ashtpadi 17 look like?
o: find a better source and post again.
log off and do one true thing.
games.why: Guru Nanak puts truthful living above truth itself. the wallet returned says more than the forty-first reply.

practice: Let the day ahead pass in front of you, the meetings, the messages, the errands, and look for one place where a small truth could be done: an honest answer, a fair share, a promise kept, a mistake owned.
Choose it, and picture your hands doing it. Then let the plan rest and just breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sachiaaraa, a truthful one. Sach aachaar: truth is high, and higher still is truthful living. Japji's first question asks how to become sachiaaraa.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sachiaaraa, truthful one, from Japji's first question, kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai.

carryVoice: Your line: truth lived. Higher than truth itself is truthful living. That's day five hundred five.
